title: About
text:
Interpretability experiments on language models. The recurring move: write down the simplest possible mathematical model of some LLM behaviour, then test it with carefully designed experiments. The simple models might be wrong in interesting ways — and the wrongness is what teaches you something about what the model is actually doing.
Everything here reproduces on a laptop. The models I use are GPT-2 small (124M) and the smaller Pythia variants (70M, 160M), chosen so experiments run in minutes, not hours.
Code

First-time setup
cd ~/Desktop/eigenation/AI

# Start a clean git repo (removes the partial one and re-inits cleanly)
rm -rf .git
git init
git add -A
git commit -m "Initial commit: Quarto blog source"
git branch -M main

Create the GitHub repo + push
If you have the GitHub CLI (gh) installed and logged in — easiest:
gh repo create probing-small-lms --public --source=. --remote=origin --push
Otherwise, do it manually:

Go to https://github.com/new
Name the repo probing-small-lms, set it Public, and do not add a README/.gitignore (you already have them). Click Create.
Back in Terminal (replace YOURNAME with your GitHub username):

git remote add origin https://github.com/YOURNAME/probing-small-lms.git
git push -u origin main


Publish the rendered site
quarto publish gh-pages
Answer yes when it asks to publish. Quarto renders the site, pushes it to a gh-pages branch, and configures GitHub Pages for you.
Your site goes live at:
https://YOURNAME.github.io/probing-small-lms/
(Give it 1–2 minutes the first time.)

Re-publishing after you edit posts
Just two commands whenever you change content:
git add -A && git commit -m "Update posts" && git push   # save source
quarto publish gh-pages                                   # rebuild + deploy

Notes

_site/ and .quarto/ are git-ignored on purpose — quarto publish rebuilds them and pushes the output to the separate gh-pages branch.
If GitHub Pages isn’t showing, check repo Settings → Pages: source should be the gh-pages branch, root folder. Quarto usually sets this automatically.
Want a custom domain (e.g. yourdomain.com)? Tell me and I’ll walk you through the CNAME setup.

title: Does GPT-2 know how big a galaxy is?
text:
In an earlier post I showed that GPT-2 small’s token embedding represents integer magnitude on a roughly logarithmic axis (R^2 = 0.95 for \log_2(x)). The natural generalisation: does the same model represent physical magnitude — sizes, durations, masses — on similar axes?
It’s not obvious which way this should go. On one hand, GPT-2 has read text about atoms (10^{-10} m), humans (\sim 1 m), and galaxies (10^{21} m). A unified “small-to-big” axis would let the model encode 30 orders of magnitude in a single direction, which is efficient. On the other hand, words like electron, kilogram, galaxy, and marathon are first particles, units, celestial bodies, and races; their mass or length is a secondary attribute that the language model may or may not have factored out into a clean direction.
To test, I assembled three lists of physical entities with known SI values:

Length (19 entities, log₁₀ spanning -10 to +21): atom, virus, cell, meter, inch, mile, marathon, earth, sun, lightyear, parsec, galaxy, etc.
Time (13 entities, log₁₀ from -9 to +10.5): nanosecond, millisecond, second, minute, hour, day, month, year, decade, century, millennium, etc.
Mass (13 entities, log₁₀ from -30 to +30): electron, proton, gram, ounce, pound, kilogram, ton, elephant, whale, earth, sun.

For each entity I take the embedding of " {name}" (single space prefix) and use the last token’s residual at layer 0. With small datasets I use leave-one-out cross-validation on a ridge probe.
The two hypotheses being tested:

H1 (separate axes). Each physical dimension has its own log axis, not shared with the others. Probes trained on one don’t transfer.
H2 (unit-agnostic magnitude). There is a shared “small-to-big” direction; the same probe works across length, time, and mass.

title: Does GPT-2 know how big a galaxy is?
text:
The result






Figure 1: Probing physical-scale axes in GPT-2 small. Top: within-category scatter of leave-one-out probe predictions vs true log₁₀(value). Time tracks the diagonal closely (R^2 = 0.81); length is messy; mass is nearly random. Bottom left: cross-category transfer matrix. Diagonal entries are within-category leave-one-out R²; off-diagonal entries are train-on-one, test-on-another. Bottom middle: combined probe across all three categories (R^2 = 0.26). Time is encoded on a clear log axis. Length is mostly noise. Mass is essentially random.
Cross-category transfer is mostly negative, with one exception: time → mass gives R^2 = +0.19, which is barely above zero but more than the others. The combined probe across all 45 entities gives R^2 = 0.26 — there’s some shared structure, but it’s weak.
So both hypotheses lose: there is no clean unit-agnostic axis, but neither do the per-category axes individually work well. The model has a clean log-time axis, weak log-length, no log-mass.

title: Does GPT-2 know how big a galaxy is?
section: Why time works and the others don’t
text:
Why time works and the others don’t
The first thing to ask is whether time is special because of physics or because of language. I think it’s mostly language. Time words form a conventional one-dimensional ladder in English:

nanosecond → microsecond → millisecond → second → minute → hour → day → week → month → year → decade → century → millennium

These tokens are functionally interchangeable in many contexts — "for five {time-word}" parses for almost every entry in that ladder. The embedding can therefore afford to compress them along a single “duration” direction, because almost everything else about these words is shared (they’re all temporal units modifying durations and frequencies).
Length and mass don’t have an analogous unidimensional ladder. The “length words” I used are a mix of:

Units of measurement: millimeter, inch, meter, mile, lightyear, parsec
Objects characterised primarily by length scale: atom, virus, cell, galaxy
Specific entities: earth, sun, moon, marathon

These belong to different semantic categories. The embedding of atom probably encodes “this is a kind of particle” more strongly than “this is 10^{-10} m long”. The embedding of marathon encodes “this is a race” more strongly than “this is 42 km”.
Mass is worse still. electron, proton, and neutron are subatomic particles; gram, ounce, pound, kilogram, ton are units; elephant, whale are animals; earth, sun are celestial bodies. The mass-magnitude attribute these all share is a tertiary feature, not something the embedding has factored out into a clean direction.






NoteThe cleaner test, which I haven’t run



If this hypothesis is right, then probing mass with disambiguating context should rescue the result. For each entity, instead of just the bare token, use a prompt like "The mass of a typical {entity} is" and probe the residual at the final token. The model is then forced to think about mass, not entity identity, so the magnitude representation should be cleaner. Same trick should help length too. I’ll come back to this.

title: Does GPT-2 know how big a galaxy is?
section: What it tells you about LLM “physics intuition”
text:
What it tells you about LLM “physics intuition”
A claim you sometimes see: large language models have learned a coherent physical world model from text. Whatever else this means, it would have to include something like a shared magnitude axis — knowing that “galactic” things are big in both length and mass, that “atomic” things are small in both, that “millennial” describes long times.
This experiment is the smallest possible test of that claim, and the result is: GPT-2 small has built a clean axis for time but not for length or mass. The unit-agnostic “small to big” axis is at best very weakly present (combined R^2 = 0.26 across 45 entities), and the per-category transfer is mostly negative.
I want to be careful about how much weight this puts on the negative claim. The test uses unembellished token embeddings, no context, and a small entity list. It tests whether the LLM has the axes “for free”, at the very first layer. Almost certainly:

A bigger model would do better. Pythia-1.4B and Llama would have more capacity to factor magnitude out from category.
A model probed with context would do better. The “mass of an elephant” context steers the residual stream toward representing mass specifically.
A model probed later in the network would do better. By layer 12 the transformer has integrated context with the token; that probably combines “this is an elephant” + relevant magnitude knowledge.

So the right summary is: at the embedding layer, GPT-2 has built a clean log-time axis but has not factored magnitude out from length-related and mass-related token semantics. The model has time-scale intuition more readily than length-scale or mass-scale intuition, because temporal nouns in English happen to form a clean one-dimensional ladder.

title: Does GPT-2 know how big a galaxy is?
section: A specific prediction — and the test
text:
A specific prediction — and the test
The hypothesis above predicts that contextualised probing should rescue length and mass. If I prompt "The mass of a typical {entity} is about" instead of feeding the bare entity word, then by the time the residual stream reaches the last token ("about"), the model has been told what quantity to think about. The magnitude information that was hiding behind category should now surface on a probe-friendly direction.
To test, I re-ran the experiment with context. For each category, the prompt template is "The {size|duration|mass} of a typical {entity} is about", and I probe the residual stream at the last token, across all layers.






ImportantPrediction confirmed



Going from bare-token probing to contextualised probing, the mass R² jumps from 0.45 to 0.84 (best layer). Time goes from 0.88 to 0.95. Length from 0.30 to 0.48. The model has the magnitude information; the bare token just doesn’t store it on a probe-friendly direction.








Figure 2: Layer-by-layer leave-one-out R² for \log_{10}(\text{SI value}), in two conditions: bare entity token (blue) versus contextualised prompt at the last token (red). For all three categories, contextualised probing reaches a higher peak R². The largest jump is for mass (0.45 → 0.84), confirming that the bare token was hiding magnitude behind semantic category. The layer profile is also informative: bare-token time peaks at layer 2 (embedding-level info), while contextualised probes peak near the final layer (context integration).



The layer profile of each curve tells a small mechanistic story:

Bare time peaks at layer 2 and gradually declines through later layers — the magnitude information sits in the embedding itself and gets diluted by subsequent processing. The temporal ladder really is built into how the tokenizer/embedding handles these words.
Contextualised time, length, and mass all peak at the final layer (or close to it). The context-driven magnitude representation is built up across the network, not present at the embedding.
Bare mass rises from R^2 = 0.03 at layer 0 to 0.45 at layer 9 before falling back. Even without context, the transformer recovers some mass-magnitude representation by mid-network — though much less than with context.

The cleanest summary: GPT-2 has rich physical-magnitude knowledge across all three categories, but only time stores it at the embedding layer. Length and mass require context-driven processing through the layers to extract their magnitude information. The asymmetry was real, but the right diagnosis isn’t “the model doesn’t know” — it’s “the model knows but needs the right question to surface it”.

title: Does GPT-2 know how big a galaxy is?
text:
What’s next
With the context-rescue result in hand, the obvious follow-ups shift:
Dimensional analysis. Does GPT-2 have a “units” axis? For prompts like "velocity has units of", can it predict the right answer? Can the model distinguish m/s (a velocity) from m·s (a strange quantity) in its internal representations? A probe along the lines of “given the residual stream, can you predict the dimensional formula?” would test the model’s grasp of unit composition.
Order-of-magnitude estimation. Standard Fermi questions (“How many piano tuners are there in Chicago?”) test the model’s ability to multiply rough estimates in head. If the integer-multiplication shortcut work I did earlier extends, the model should handle these via log-axis addition.
Scale-ladder representation across modalities. If we could combine text + image embeddings (e.g., in CLIP or a multimodal LLM), is there a “scale” axis that lines up across image of atom and image of galaxy? The conjecture: in a model trained on enough multimodal data, yes, because images come with implicit scale cues (microscope, telescope, etc.).
Test the linguistic-ladder hypothesis directly. Take a bunch of abstract concept categories where the words do form a clean ladder (temperature: cold, cool, warm, hot, boiling; speed: slow, crawling, walking, running, sprinting, flying). The probe should work cleanly on these for the same reason it worked on time. Categories without a ladder (length, mass) should fail. This isolates the linguistic mechanism.

title: Does GPT-2 know how big a galaxy is?
text:
Code

probe_gpt2_physics.py — bare-token experiment.
probe_gpt2_physics_context.py — contextualised experiment, with the layer-by-layer comparison.

Both reproduce in about a minute on CPU.

The “GPT-2 knows physics” narrative needs a careful unpacking. The model has all three* magnitude axes when you ask in the right way (R^2 \in [0.48, 0.95]). But only time has its magnitude stored right at the embedding ladder. Length and mass require the network to do context-driven work across many layers to extract the same information. The takeaway for probing methodology: a negative result from bare-token probing tells you about the embedding, not about the model’s knowledge.*

title: Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model
text:
For three centuries before the pocket calculator, engineers multiplied with slide rules. The slide rule is a physical implementation of one identity:

a \cdot b = 2^{\log_2 a + \log_2 b}
\tag{1}
Three lookups and an addition, instead of a multiplication. The trick rests on a different geometry of number — positions on the slide rule are spaced by \log_2, not by raw magnitude, so adding two distances corresponds to multiplying the underlying values.
Does a neural network ever discover this geometry? If you train a model to predict text and it sees enough numbers, does it secretly learn the slide rule?
There’s a longer plan in experiment1.md to train a fresh tiny Transformer from scratch under capacity pressure and dissect it — Anthropic-style mechanistic interpretability. That’s weeks of work. This post is the parallel and cheaper question: is the shortcut already sitting inside an existing small language model?
To find out, I poked at GPT-2 small (the 124M-parameter model from 2019) and Pythia-160M (a more modern but similarly-sized model) with two tools: linear probes (a regression that reads a value off the residual stream) and activation patching (an intervention that surgically changes one direction in the residual stream and watches what happens downstream).






NoteSummary in one figure









Figure 1: Six panels covering three models (GPT-2 small / Pythia-70M / Pythia-160M). A: Embedding log-axis decodability in all three. Log dominates only under weight tying; untied Pythia models prefer linear by a hair. B: GPT-2 does compute \log_2(a \cdot b) at the equals-sign at R^2 = 0.989 — but on a different axis than the one used to read the operands. C: New result. Patching along that fresh answer-side direction moves the LM head’s argmax with slope only 0.07 — the probe is correlational, not causal. D: LM-head log-axis fraction collapses to baseline once weights are untied, so GPT-2’s “28× baseline” was mostly architectural. E: Near-miss slope \beta is invariant at ~0.22 across all three models, even as panels A and D vary by orders of magnitude. F: synthesis.

title: Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model
section: A simple model first: when should a learner discover the shortcut?
text:
A simple model first: when should a learner discover the shortcut?
Before touching real models I built a toy that makes the cost-pressure hypothesis quantitative. Two paths can compute z = a \cdot b:

Direct multiplication, with cost c_{\mathrm{mul}}(a, b) = \log_2(a) \cdot \log_2(b) — bit × bit schoolbook work. 2 \times 2 is one bit times one bit; 1024 \times 512 is ten bits times nine.
The log–sum–exp shortcut, with cost c_{\mathrm{short}} = 6 — three primitive operations, independent of operand size.

A learnable gate p \in [0, 1] reads (\log_2 a, \log_2 b) and picks how much shortcut to use. The expected total cost at penalty weight \lambda is

C(p, a, b, \lambda) = (1-p)\cdot \lambda \cdot c_{\mathrm{mul}}(a, b) + p \cdot c_{\mathrm{short}}.
\tag{2}
Sweep \lambda. The aggregate probability of taking the shortcut traces a smooth sigmoid. The interesting geometry is in which (a, b) pairs switch first — hard ones do, easy ones hold out, and trivial ones (those involving 1) never switch, because \log_2(1) = 0 makes direct multiplication genuinely free.






Figure 2: Toy soft-routing model under varying multiplication-penalty weight \lambda. Top: average shortcut probability across (a, b) \in [1, 64]^2. The trained gate matches the analytical softmin to three decimal places. Bottom: per-pair gate at five snapshot \lambda values; the decision boundary sweeps from upper-right (hard pairs) to lower-left (easy pairs) as the penalty grows.



This isn’t itself a finding. It’s a yardstick — the routing geometry predicted by the simplest possible cost-cutter. The empirical question is whether real language models trained on text, not on multiplication, show even a faint trace of this geometry.

title: Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model
text:
How GPT-2 represents numbers
To check what a model has internalised about integers, take the residual stream — the model’s internal scratchpad at each layer — at the position of a number token, and ask: can a linear regression predict \log_2(x) from it? If yes, the model has a “log of this number” axis at that layer.
I fed GPT-2 small the integers 2 through 1023, each as " 5", " 17", " 1024", etc. Most are single BPE tokens. At every layer I extracted the residual stream and trained a ridge probe for \log_2(x) and several controls.
At the very first layer — the raw token embedding, before any transformer block has run — \log_2(x) is decodable at R^2 = 0.95 on held-out integers. Raw x is also decodable, but worse, at R^2 = 0.77. Shuffled labels (a noise control) give R^2 \approx 0. So the embedding prefers the log shape.
To confirm the axis is really log-shaped and not just “any monotone function of x”, I swept the power-law family x^\alpha. Decodability peaks right around \alpha = 0 — the log limit. If GPT-2 stored linear magnitude the peak would sit at \alpha = 1. It doesn’t.
What’s more surprising is what else the embedding stores. Parity is decodable at R^2 = 0.94. Last digit (x \bmod 10) at R^2 = 0.92. GPT-2 has noticed, just from reading text, that " 5", " 15", " 25" all share the feature of ending in 5. Ask the same probe for "is x divisible by 7?" and the R^2 is essentially zero. Same for "is x prime?". The embedding has structure for the things a careful reader of natural language might track — size, parity, last digit — and ignores number-theory properties that show up too rarely in text to matter.






Figure 3: Linear-probe R^2 at each layer for monotone targets, non-monotone targets, and a noise baseline. The log axis, parity, and last digit are all decodable at the embedding (R^2 > 0.9). Number-theoretic properties (mod 7, primality) and the shuffle control are at chance.




Does this generalise across categories of numbers?
A natural question: does the integer log axis carry over to other numeric tokens — years like " 1990", round numbers like " 1000", number-words like " million"? A simple model says yes: GPT-2 has one shared magnitude axis for everything numeric.
The data says no, decisively. Apply the integer-trained probe to:

152 single-token years from [1500, 2099] → R^2 = -2274. The readouts are nearly constant regardless of which year you feed in. The integer axis can’t distinguish 1500 from 2099 at all.
33 single-token round numbers (multiples of 100 up to 100 000) → R^2 = 0.22. Weak positive transfer.
24 single-token English number-words (“one”…“twenty”, “hundred”, “thousand”, “million”, “billion”) → R^2 = 0.14.







Figure 4: The integer-trained log probe applied to other numeric categories. Integers (training) sit cleanly on y = x. Years, round numbers, and number-words sit far off the line. Each numeric category lives on its own axis in embedding space; there is no universal magnitude direction.



This tells you something about how GPT-2 represents numbers. The token " 1990" is encoded primarily as “a year” — its role in text — and only weakly as “the number 1990”. The model’s representation is role-dependent, not value-dependent. A probe trained on integers reads years as nonsense.

title: Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model
section: Does the log axis actually do anything?
text:
Does the log axis actually do anything?
Decodability is a correlational fact. To test whether the model uses the log axis when it multiplies, I ran activation patching at the operand token.
Take a prompt like " 5 * 9 =". The model processes it normally. At the position where " 5" sits, the embedding’s projection onto the probe direction w reads \log_2(5) \approx 2.3. I add a rank-1 vector along w so that projection now reads \log_2(2) = 1. Everything else about the embedding stays the same — same parity, same last-digit, same noise. Then I let the model run the full 12 layers and ask: which numeric token does the next-token distribution prefer?
For " 5 * 9 =", patching \log_2(5) \to \log_2(2) makes the logit for " 18" (= 2 \cdot 9) rise above the logit for " 45" (= 5 \cdot 9). The model has been talked into preferring the patched product. Patching toward 4 makes " 36" win. Patching toward 5 does nothing, as it should. And — the critical control — patching along five different random directions of equal magnitude to w gives logit shifts indistinguishable from zero. The effect is specific to the probe direction.
The effect is also asymmetric. Patching downward (toward smaller numbers) works cleanly. Patching upward (toward larger numbers) only partly works. Most plausible explanation: the LM head has a strong frequency prior favouring small, common numbers in text. A fixed-size patch is enough to push preference toward smaller numbers (with the prior) but not enough to push it toward larger numbers (against the prior).






Figure 5: Causal patching at the operand position. Left: change in relative logit, \mathrm{logit}(a_{\mathrm{target}} \cdot b) - \mathrm{logit}(a \cdot b), as we patch the log direction at the " a" position. Solid lines are the log direction; dotted lines are random directions of the same norm. Right: heatmap of relative logits for " 5 * 9 =". The yellow most-favoured-product stripe follows the perfect-log-shortcut line p = a_{\mathrm{target}} \cdot b for downward patches, then sticks at 45 once we patch toward larger numbers.

title: Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model
section: Does the model actually compute log(a·b)?
text:
Does the model actually compute log(a·b)?
This is the test I most wanted to run.
If the model does the slide-rule trick — adds the operand logs and then exponentiates at the end — then at the position of the = sign, the residual stream right before the LM head should be carrying \log_2(a \cdot b). The operand-side log direction w ought to read off this value.
I checked. For " 5 * 9 =", the operand-side probe at = reads off 10.76 — not \log_2(45) \approx 5.49. For " 3 * 7 =" it reads 11.17, not \log_2(21) \approx 4.39. Across nine different prompts, the readout is essentially flat. The R^2 of “what the operand-axis probe reads at =” against “the true \log_2(a \cdot b)” is 0.011 — no signal.
My first reaction was that the circuit isn’t there. The shortcut exists on the input side, but the model isn’t wiring it together.
Then it occurred to me: maybe the model uses a different direction at the = position to write down the answer’s log than the one it uses to read the operands’ logs. There’s no architectural reason those have to be the same vector — the model can translate between representations as it computes. So I trained a fresh ridge probe directly on the residual at =, against \log_2(a \cdot b) for several hundred random (a, b) pairs.






ImportantThe key result



The new probe predicts the answer’s log at R^2 = 0.989 on held-out (a, b) pairs. The model has computed \log_2(a \cdot b). It’s there. It’s almost perfectly linearly decodable from the residual stream right before the LM head. I had simply been looking on the wrong axis.


So the picture is this. The operands’ logs are written down on one axis at the input. Somewhere in the middle layers, the model adds them and rewrites the result on a different axis at the = position. The LM head then reads that second axis to decide what number comes next. The whole \log \to \mathrm{sum} \to \exp machine is sitting in GPT-2 small.






Figure 6: The end-to-end pipeline. Left: patching the log component at the = position of real prompts; argmax over numeric tokens is stuck at " 1" regardless of v_{\mathrm{target}}. Middle: the operand-side probe’s readout at = is roughly constant (\sim 10.8) across all prompts, uncorrelated with \log_2(a \cdot b) (R^2 = 0.011). Right: a fresh probe trained directly on residuals at = predicts \log_2(a \cdot b) at R^2 = 0.989 on held-out pairs.




A correction: the answer-side direction is correlational, not causal
The R^2 = 0.989 number is striking enough that I should ask whether the direction the probe found is actually the one the model uses, rather than some downstream feature that correlates with \log_2(a \cdot b). That’s the classic correlation-vs-causation issue with linear probes, sometimes called the “probing illusion”.
The clean way to test causation: take the fitted answer-side direction w_{\mathrm{ans}}, then for various v_{\mathrm{target}}, patch the residual at = so the projection onto w_{\mathrm{ans}} equals v_{\mathrm{target}}, apply the LM head, and check whether the argmax over numeric tokens tracks 2^{v_{\mathrm{target}}}.
If the model uses this direction, the LM head’s argmax should follow 2^{v_{\mathrm{target}}} — slope 1 on a log-log plot. If it merely correlates with \log_2(a \cdot b), patching it should move nothing.
The result: slope 0.072, not 1. For most prompts the argmax over numeric tokens doesn’t change at all across an 11-log-unit sweep. The LM head clearly doesn’t read this direction. The 0.989 R² says \log_2(a \cdot b) is encoded there — but probably as a downstream consequence of whatever the model is actually doing, not because the LM head reads it.






WarningHonest revision



The original write-up of this experiment claimed the pipeline was “wired up” because the answer’s log was decodable at R^2 = 0.989. The causal test shows that’s overclaiming. The decodability is real, but the LM head doesn’t act on that specific direction. The right summary is: the model has computed something equivalent to \log_2(a \cdot b) somewhere in its residual stream at =, but the LM head’s actual choice of next token is driven by other directions. What those directions encode, and how they relate to the operand-side log axis, is still open.








Figure 7: Patching along the fitted answer-side direction w_{\mathrm{ans}} at the = position. Left: for each of eight multiplication prompts, \log_2 of the LM head’s argmax-numeric vs the injected v_{\mathrm{target}}. Compared to the dashed reference y = v_{\mathrm{target}}, the curves are essentially flat — the LM head doesn’t read this direction. Right: rank of the closest single-token integer to 2^{v_{\mathrm{target}}} among all numeric tokens. The target never ends up at rank 0; it bottoms around 100-300 out of 638 numeric tokens.

title: Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model
section: Two more checks: was the other finding real or an artifact?
text:
Two more checks: was the other finding real or an artifact?
The 0.989 number is striking enough that I want to ask twice. Two follow-ups, both quantitative.

Check 1 — does the LM head act on the log axis?
The LM head’s row for each numeric token is what gets dotted with the residual stream to produce the next-token logit. If the log axis matters for output, those rows should have non-trivial mass on it.
For GPT-2 small: the log direction captures 3.6% of each numeric LM-head row’s squared norm on average, versus 1/d = 0.13\% for a random direction — about 28\times the isotropic baseline.
But there’s a catch. GPT-2 ties its LM head to its embedding, so the LM head row for token " 5" is literally the same vector as the embedding of " 5". The “alignment” of LM head with log axis is automatic, not emergent. To separate “tying” from “emergent alignment”, I re-ran the analysis on two more models with untied weights — Pythia-70M and Pythia-160M:

Without weight tying, the LM head doesn’t independently align with the integer-embedding log axis. The underlying log axis is real (decodable at R^2 \approx 0.89 in both Pythia embeddings too — see panel A of Figure 1), but the LM head doesn’t inherit it for free when weights are untied. The “28× baseline” number for GPT-2 was largely an artifact of weight tying.






Figure 8: LM-head log-axis decomposition for GPT-2 small. The 3.6% number averaged over numeric tokens is real, but the comparison with Pythia (see panel C of Figure 1) shows most of that comes from weight tying.





Check 2 — does the log axis pull on the actual output distribution?
The behavioural test. For 200 random multiplication prompts (a, b) \in [2, 50)^2, I look at the model’s next-token distribution restricted to numeric tokens, and fit a simple log-Gaussian:

P(\text{predict } n \mid a, b) \propto \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\log_2 n - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
\tag{3}
If the log circuit drives output, \mu \approx \log_2(a \cdot b) and \sigma shrinks with confidence. If the log axis is ignored, \mu has no relation to the true log.
The result sits between these. Across 200 prompts:

0/200 argmaxes are correct (GPT-2 small really can’t multiply).
Fitted \mu is biased \mathbf{-3.25} log-units below the true \log_2(a \cdot b) on average. The model predicts numbers about 2^{3.25} \approx 9.5\times smaller than the right answer.
But the slope of \mu vs \log_2(a \cdot b) across prompts is \boldsymbol{\beta = 0.22}. Not 1 (perfect readout), not 0 (no readout), but a clear positive coupling.

Repeating the experiment on Pythia-70M gives \beta = 0.22 — same as GPT-2. On Pythia-160M I get \beta = 0.19. Across three models with very different LM-head geometries (4 orders of magnitude apart in their log-axis fraction), the behavioural pull on output is the same: about 22% of what a clean readout would produce. The slope \beta \approx
0.22 looks like a property of the cost-sensitive output distribution the models share, not of how their LM heads happen to align with integer-embedding directions.

The mean predicted log tracks the true log with slope \beta = 0.22, biased about 3 units below the y = x line. Middle: fitted spread \sigma is roughly constant at \sim 1.9 log-units. Right: three example predicted distributions; dotted vertical lines mark the true \log_2(a \cdot b).



This \beta = 0.22 ties everything together. The log circuit puts \log_2(a \cdot b) in the residual stream at R^2 = 0.989. The LM head acts on it to roughly 22% of what perfect readout would give, swamped by a much larger frequency prior. The machine is wired up; it just isn’t loud enough.

title: Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model
text:
What this collectively shows
Five claims, the first three robust and the last two more tentative.
The embedding layer of all three models encodes integers on an approximately logarithmic axis, along with separate axes for parity and last digit. Number-theoretic properties not visible in surface text (mod 7, primality) do not get a coherent representation. The log-axis shape peaks the power-law sweep at \alpha = 0, but the absolute preference of log over linear is partly weight-tying dependent — GPT-2 has log \gg linear at the embedding, while untied Pythia models have log \approx linear there.
Perturbations along the embedding’s log axis have structured, direction-specific causal effect on the model’s next-token predictions in multiplication prompts. Random directions of the same magnitude do not. This rules out the “probe is finding a noise direction” null hypothesis. The asymmetry of the effect (downward patches work, upward patches partly fail) points at the LM head’s frequency prior as the limiting factor.
In all three models, the behavioural pull of the log axis on actual output is invariant at \beta \approx 0.22 — about 22% of what perfect log-circuit readout would give. This is true across models that differ by orders of magnitude in their LM-head log-axis alignment. So the behavioural number isn’t a function of LM-head geometry; it’s a function of how loud the output-side frequency prior is relative to whatever the log circuit contributes.
A fresh probe trained on =-position residuals to predict \log_2(a \cdot b) achieves R^2 = 0.989 on held-out pairs. The model has computed something linearly equivalent to the answer’s log somewhere in its residual stream. But patching that direction barely moves the LM head’s argmax (slope 0.07 of perfect readout). So the direction is a downstream encoding, not the one the head actually reads. What direction the head does read for numeric output, and how it relates to the operand-side log axis, is the most interesting open question this work leaves.
The framing-level lesson is that small language models can have mechanistically rich circuits whose behavioural effect is suppressed by the output distribution they were trained against. “Can’t do multiplication” is consistent with “has parts of the multiplication circuit”, as long as a louder competing signal is shouting “use a common number” and the probe-found directions aren’t the ones the LM head listens to.

title: Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model
text:
Caveats
GPT-2 ties its LM head to the embedding. Much of the apparent LM head ↔︎ log axis alignment is architectural. The Pythia-160M comparison addresses this for one untied model, but a wider scan across model families would be more convincing.
The causal-patching shifts are measured on relative logits among candidate products, not on argmax. Both small models get 0/200 multiplications right. A model that can actually multiply (Pythia-1.4B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen-2.5-0.5B) would let the patch flip the argmax cleanly, not just shift relative logits.
The fitted answer-side probe at the = position has R^2 = 0.989 on (a, b) \in [2, 64]^2 pairs. Whether the same direction carries \log_2(a \cdot b) for much larger operands is untested.
The middle layers — where the operand-axis log gets translated to the answer-axis log — are a black box in this study. Path-patching across (layer, position) pairs would identify the attention heads that move log information from operand positions to the = position. The infrastructure for it is already in the patching code; I just didn’t run it.

title: Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model
text:
Five things to test next
Find the direction the LM head actually reads. The biggest open question raised by the answer-side causal test. The 0.989 probe is correlational; the LM head’s argmax is driven by some other direction. A sparse autoencoder or top-singular-vectors analysis of the LM-head columns for numeric tokens should expose what they actually decode.
Exponentiation as a sharper test. If the model uses the log axis compositionally, patching \log(a) by \Delta in an a^b = prompt should shift the output’s log by b \cdot \Delta — a quantitative prediction with one free parameter. Same patching code, different prompts.
A bigger model that can actually multiply. Pythia-1.4B, Llama-3.2-1B, or Qwen-2.5-0.5B. If \beta = 0.22 is invariant across model scale, it’s a property of the training distribution, not capacity. If \beta shoots up on a multiply-capable model, the limit at small scale really was “the head doesn’t act on the log axis hard enough”.
Path-patch to find the translation layer. Where in the network does the operand-axis log get translated to whatever ends up at =? The patching infrastructure here is already 80% of what’s needed.
Test the per-category axes. Within years, fit a year-trained log probe. Does it transfer cleanly to other years? Repeat for round numbers, number-words. If the integer-trained axis doesn’t transfer (the result above) but the within-category axes do transfer, the model has many private log axes, one per role.

title: Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model
text:
Methodological note
If a probe trained at position A gives no signal at position B, that doesn’t mean the information isn’t in B — it might just mean B uses a different direction. Fit a fresh probe at the position you actually care about before concluding the circuit is absent. In this study, that one habit was the difference between “no circuit found” and “circuit found at R^2 = 0.989”.
The shared-axis test worked the same way in reverse: an attractive hypothesis (“there’s one universal magnitude axis for all numeric tokens”) was falsified with about twenty minutes of compute and one transfer measurement. The Pythia comparison was the same shape — running the same probe on a second model with untied weights corrected a number I would otherwise have over-interpreted. Cheap probes are how you both rescue and kill ideas.

title: Transformers learn to anchor: a small experiment in positional periodicity
text:
When you train a transformer on data that has a periodic structure, its attention pattern often shows striking spikes at integer multiples of the period — 24 steps, 48 steps, 72 steps. The natural reading is that the model has learned the periodicity of the data and is “looking at” the corresponding earlier events.
But there’s a quieter, weirder possibility. The model could instead have compiled a fixed positional routine: “always look at slot 24, regardless of what’s there.” Under this story, the periodic spikes aren’t reports about which events are informative — they’re an internal indexing scheme that happens to align with the period of the data.
The two stories make very different predictions about what attention “means,” and they’re hard to tell apart in a real recommendation system, where you can’t manipulate the data without retraining and you don’t know which events actually matter. So let’s set the real system aside and run the experiment in a sandbox where we control everything.

title: Transformers learn to anchor: a small experiment in positional periodicity
text:
The setup
We train a tiny transformer (≈29k parameters, 2 layers, 1 attention head) to predict the next value of a noisy periodic signal:
y_t = \text{intercept} + \text{slope} \cdot t + A \sin(2\pi t / 24 + \phi) + \varepsilon_t
with random amplitude, phase, slope, and additive noise. The model sees the last 96 values (4 full periods) and predicts the next one.






Figure 1: Example sequences from the synthetic dataset. The red dot is the prediction target.



This task has clean optimal behavior. To predict the next value you need to estimate the trend and the phase of the sine. To estimate phase, any point in the past is informative once you know its position relative to the target — and adjacent points are nearly equally informative because the underlying sine is smooth. There’s no special reason for “exactly 24 steps ago” to matter more than “23 steps ago.”
A learnable query token is appended to the sequence; the model reads its prediction only from that position, mirroring the LLaTTE-style readout bottleneck. After 6 epochs of training the model reaches validation MSE 0.117, close to the irreducible noise floor (~0.09), and well below the predict-last-value baseline (0.210).

title: Transformers learn to anchor: a small experiment in positional periodicity
section: What the attention pattern looks like
text:
What the attention pattern looks like
We extract attention weights from the query token back to each input position, average across the layers, and then average across 1000 held-out sequences:






Figure 2: Average attention from the query token vs lag. Dashed red lines mark integer multiples of the period.



There it is. Sharp recurring spikes, roughly one period apart, plus a strong recency peak near lag 1. The model has learned positional anchoring.
A couple of details worth flagging now, since they’ll matter for the interventions:

The anchors are slightly off the literal period. The peaks sit at lags 23, 45, 69, not 24, 48, 72. This is itself a hint of B: the data’s period is exactly 24, but the model picked something else. Why? My best guess: causal attention favors looking into the past rather than at the period boundary; lag 23 gives almost the same phase information as lag 24 but is one step deeper into the predictive horizon. Either way, the discrepancy means the spike locations are a learned implementation detail, not a transcription of the data’s period.
Lag 23 gets ~13× more attention than lag 22. A zoom-in:







Figure 3: Zoomed view around the lag-23 spike. The dashed red line is the literal period; the spike is one step before it.



Two adjacent positions, near-identical content, very different attention weight. This is the configuration the swap experiment will exploit.
So far everything is consistent with both interpretations. The model could be paying attention at lag 23 because it has learned that the period-aligned point is informative (A), or because it has compiled a positional reading routine (B). Time to disambiguate.

title: Transformers learn to anchor: a small experiment in positional periodicity
section: Intervention 1: shift the period, watch the attention
text:
Intervention 1: shift the period, watch the attention
If the model is tracking the periodic signal in the data, then changing where the period actually aligns should move the attention spikes. Concretely: we generate sequences where the prediction target sits 4 steps after the input window (instead of 1 step after, as in training). Now the “one period before target” point sits at lag 21 from the end of the input window, not lag 24. Under A, the spike should follow the signal. Under B, the spike stays where the model put it.






Figure 4: Attention pattern under baseline (predict t+1) and offset target (predict t+4). The two curves overlap completely.



You can only see one curve because the two are exactly on top of each other — the baseline and offset attention patterns are identical to ~3 decimal places at every lag. The model’s attention pattern is completely insensitive to where the period actually aligns relative to the target.
Meanwhile prediction MSE went from 0.117 to 0.403 — a 3.4× degradation. The model is paying a real cost for keeping its attention pinned to the wrong positions. It would benefit from moving the spikes, and it doesn’t.
This rules out the strongest form of A. The attention pattern is not “wherever the period-aligned points happen to be.” It’s wherever the model has learned to look.

title: Transformers learn to anchor: a small experiment in positional periodicity
text:
Intervention 2: swap the contents
OK, but maybe the model has just learned a fixed positional routine that usually aligns with the period and treats the value at that position as informative. In that case, the value at the anchor position should still matter to the model. We can test this by leaving the anchor position alone but changing what value sits there.
The anchor is at lag 23. Its near neighbor at lag 22 carries essentially the same information (autocorrelation between adjacent points in a sine with period 24 is ~0.97). We do two interventions:

Swap. Exchange the values at lag 22 and lag 23. Position 23 now holds what used to be at position 22 (similar but not identical value); position 22 now holds the old anchor value. If attention is following informative content, it should move to position 22.
Corrupt. Replace the value at lag 23 with random Gaussian noise. If attention reflects informativeness, it should drop (the value is now uninformative).







Figure 5: Three attention curves — baseline, after value swap, and after value corruption — all overlap.



Three curves, one shape. The attention pattern is unchanged under both interventions, down to the third decimal. Numerically:

Note the small increase in attention after corruption. The model didn’t just fail to redirect attention away from a now-meaningless slot — it slightly increased the weight. The anchor position is a routine, not a referendum on what’s there.
The prediction MSE tells a coherent story:



Table 2: Prediction MSE under each intervention. The model cannot route around a broken anchor.

Corruption hurts noticeably, because the model is still reading from the corrupted position and is now putting noise into its prediction. It cannot route around the broken anchor.

title: Transformers learn to anchor: a small experiment in positional periodicity
section: What this shows, and what it doesn’t
text:
What this shows, and what it doesn’t
In this controlled setting the model very clearly does Interpretation B. Periodic attention spikes are positional anchors, not pointers at informative events. The evidence:

The spikes don’t sit on the literal period (lag 23, not lag 24).
They don’t move when the period of the data shifts.
They don’t move when the values at those positions are swapped or replaced with noise.
The model pays a measurable prediction cost rather than redirecting attention.

What this does not show, in order of importance:

This isn’t a refutation of A in real systems. Real user behavior has genuine routines — people do click ads at the same time of day. A model trained on real data probably learns both a periodic anchoring strategy and picks up on event-level signal. The experiment shows that anchoring is a thing transformers can learn purely from positional cues; it doesn’t quantify how much of any real attention pattern is anchoring vs. content.
The synthetic data is much simpler than user behavior. With a single dominant frequency and Gaussian noise, the cheapest strategy may genuinely be “anchor on the period and reconstruct.” Real sequences have multiple time scales, irregular spacing, and heterogeneous content; the cost-benefit tradeoff for anchoring is different. I’d expect anchoring to be less extreme there, with more content-sensitivity mixed in.
One model, one seed, one period. I didn’t sweep architectures or seeds. The qualitative finding (positional anchors exist and dominate attention) was robust enough to show up clearly on the first training run, but the precise lag of the spikes is an implementation detail of this particular run.
The anchoring is causally consequential. Corruption of the anchor degrades MSE; the model can’t compensate. This is the part that should make us cautious about interpreting attention as “what the model thinks is informative.” The model thinks the slot is informative — and is wrong, in a way it can’t correct.

title: Transformers learn to anchor: a small experiment in positional periodicity
text:
The takeaway
I find this useful as a calibration. The next time someone shows me an attention plot with sharp periodic spikes and a story about temporal patterns, I’ll want to know: did anyone test whether the spikes move when the periodic alignment moves? Did anyone swap the contents of the spike positions? If not, the plot is consistent with the model having learned a clever indexing scheme that has nothing to do with the temporal narrative.
It’s also a reminder that interpretability is hard in a specific way. The attention pattern isn’t telling us what the model thinks; it’s telling us what the model does. Translating from “does” to “thinks” requires interventions, and in this small example the two come out genuinely different.

title: Notes on what language models know about the world
text:
Each post here uses a small, runnable experiment — linear probes, activation patching, simple closed-form models — to ask one question about how a language model represents some piece of the world. The emphasis is on cheap and direct: every figure here reproduces on a laptop pc in under an hour.
The posts:

Does GPT-2 know how big a galaxy is?


Probing a small language model for physical-scale intuitions across length, time, and mass — and finding that one of these is encoded cleanly and the other two aren’t.



interpretability

physics

language models



A natural extension of the integer-magnitude axis I found in GPT-2’s embedding: does the same model represent physical magnitude — sizes, durations, masses — on a log axis? Probing 45 entities spanning many orders of magnitude in each of three categories, I find a clean asymmetry. Time is represented on a log axis with held-out R^2 = 0.81. Length is weak (R^2 = 0.18). Mass is essentially noise (R^2 = 0.03). Cross-category transfer is mostly negative. The reason is mostly linguistic, not physical: time words form a conventional one-dimensional ladder of duration (nanosecond → minute → year → millennium), so the embedding can compress them onto a single axis. Length and mass words are semantically heterogeneous — kilogram, elephant, and electron are first a unit, an animal, and a particle, and only secondarily masses — so the embedding ends up encoding category rather than magnitude.





May 6, 2024


Huangxing Li












Looking for the log-multiplication trick inside a small language model


Where does GPT-2 keep its slide rule? A tour through linear probes, activation patching, and one large surprise.



interpretability

mech-interp

language models

arithmetic



Before pocket calculators, scientists multiplied with slide rules: look up two logarithms, add them, look up an exponential. Does a language model ever do the same? Using linear probes and activation patching on three small language models (GPT-2 small, Pythia-70M, Pythia-160M), I find that (1) the token embedding represents integer magnitude on a roughly logarithmic axis (R^2 = 0.89-0.95); (2) perturbing this axis has direction-specific causal effect on multiplication predictions, rulingß out generic noise; (3) the answer’s log is linearly decodable from the residual stream at the equals-sign position with R^2 = 0.989 — but patching along that direction barely moves the LM head’s output (causal slope 0.07), so the probe finding is correlational, not the direction the model actually uses; and (4) across all three models, the behavioural pull of the log axis on actual output is invariant at \beta \approx 0.22 of perfect readout, dominated by an LM-head frequency prior. The slide-rule substrate exists; the head’s free-will is small.
